title: What to Ask About HVAC When Buying a Home
h1: What Should I Ask About the HVAC System When Buying a Home?
description: Buying a home in San Diego or Orange County? Here are the HVAC questions to ask before closing, what to check yourself, and when to get an HVAC inspection.
quick_answer: Ask how old the furnace, AC and ducts are, when they were last serviced, whether any repairs or replacements were permitted, and whether any warranty transfers. Look at the equipment yourself and test heating and cooling. For older systems or any concerns, get an HVAC inspection before closing.
body:
Why does the HVAC system matter when buying a home?

Heating and cooling equipment is one of the most expensive systems in a house to replace. A general home inspection usually checks whether the system turns on and looks for obvious problems, but it often doesn't include a detailed look inside the equipment or ductwork. Knowing the system's age and condition before you close helps you budget and negotiate.

What questions should I ask the seller?

  1. How old is the furnace, air conditioner or heat pump? Ask for both the indoor and outdoor units, since they may differ.
  2. When was it last serviced? Ask for maintenance records or receipts.
  3. Have there been any major repairs? Things like compressor replacement, refrigerant leaks or heat exchanger issues.
  4. Was the system installed or replaced with a permit? Unpermitted work can cause trouble later.
  5. Is there a manufacturer warranty, and does it transfer? Some require registration or a transfer process.
  6. Have the ducts been cleaned, sealed or replaced?
  7. Are there rooms that are always too hot or cold?
  8. What refrigerant does the AC use? Older R-22 systems are costly to recharge.
  9. Have there been any pest or rodent issues in the attic?

What can I check myself during a showing or walkthrough?

  • Find the data plate on each unit and take a photo of the model and serial numbers.
  • Run the heat and the AC for several minutes each. Listen for odd noises and feel for steady airflow in each room.
  • Look at the filter. A clogged filter can be a clue about how the system has been maintained.
  • Check the outdoor unit for bent fins, rust or corrosion, which is common near the coast, and plants growing into it.
  • Look around the furnace or air handler in the garage, attic or closet for water stains, rust or scorch marks.
  • Notice smells like mustiness or burning when the system starts.
  • Peek into the attic if you can, looking for crushed or disconnected ducts and signs of rodents.

Should I get a separate HVAC inspection?

It's worth it if the system is older, the home has been vacant, the seller doesn't have service records, or anything in your own checks or the home inspection raised a question. An HVAC technician can:

  • Check the furnace heat exchanger and venting for safety concerns
  • Test refrigerant levels and electrical parts
  • Measure airflow and temperature differences
  • Inspect the ducts for leaks, damage and contamination
  • Give a realistic sense of remaining life and upcoming repairs

Ask for the inspection to include photos and a written summary so you can share it with your agent and use it in any repair requests. If the home has more than one system, such as a separate unit for an upstairs or an addition, make sure each one is checked.

Schedule it during the inspection contingency period so you have time to act on what you learn. If a home has gas appliances or an attached garage, also confirm that carbon monoxide alarms are installed, as California requires.

What should I do with what I learn?

If the system needs repairs or replacement soon, you have options. You can ask the seller to make repairs, request a credit, adjust your offer, or simply plan and budget for the work after you move in. Older homes in San Diego and Orange County may also need attic cleaning, duct replacement or insulation upgrades, which are easier to do before you move furniture in.

Keep any paperwork you get, including the inspection report, model and serial numbers, and warranty details, in one place. You'll want it the first time something needs service.

Once you own the home, start fresh: change the filter, book a tune-up if there's no recent service record, and write down the age and model of each unit so you can plan ahead.

faqs: Does a home inspection cover the HVAC system?

A general home inspection usually checks that the system runs and looks for visible problems. It typically does not include a detailed check of the heat exchanger, refrigerant or ductwork, which is why a separate HVAC inspection can help.
How old is too old for an HVAC system in a home I am buying?
There is no hard cutoff, but furnaces often last around 15 to 20 years and ACs around 12 to 15. A system near or past those ages is worth inspecting and budgeting for.
Can I ask the seller to replace the HVAC system?
You can request repairs or a credit based on inspection findings. What the seller agrees to depends on the market and your negotiations. Your real estate agent can advise on the best approach.
Should I get the ducts cleaned before moving in?
It's a good idea if the ducts are dirty, there was remodeling, the previous owners had pets or smoked, or there's evidence of rodents. It's easiest to do before you move in.
